query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a controlled elevated preheat of the build chamber during SLM of HEA components will reduce residual thermal gradients and related stresses, thereby minimizing fabrication-induced defects while enhancing dimensional accuracy and mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy (HEA) components fabricated via selective laser melting under standard conditions (i.e., without active chamber preheating), which typically exhibit rapid local cooling, residual stresses, and associated defects such as porosity and distortion.
generation.intervention: Introduce a preheating stage by maintaining the build chamber at an elevated temperature (for example, in the range of 200–400 °C) throughout the SLM fabrication process.
generation.conditions: The study is carried out using a laser powder bed fusion (SLM) system in an inert argon atmosphere. HEA parts (using either pre-alloyed or blended elemental powders) are produced with identical laser power, scan speed, and layer thickness; the only variable is the chamber temperature—baseline at ambient and experimental runs at controlled preheat levels (e.g., 200 °C, 300 °C, and 400 °C). Post-build, dimensional measurements (using 3D optical metrology) and mechanical tests (tensile and hardness tests under room temperature conditions) are performed.
generation.structural_mediator: The elevated preheat reduces thermal gradients during solidification, which in turn lowers the formation of residual stresses and minimizes defect nucleation (e.g., porosity, cracks, and distortions) while promoting a more uniform and refined microstructure.
generation.mechanism: By preheating the build chamber, the temperature difference between the molten pool and the surrounding material is decreased. This reduction in thermal gradient slows down the cooling rate, lessens internal stress build-up, and minimizes distortion. Consequently, the lower thermal shock reduces the likelihood of key defects and enhances mechanical properties by fostering a more homogeneous microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline samples, HEA components produced under preheated conditions are expected to exhibit significantly improved dimensional precision (with reduced warping and shrinkage), lower defect densities (fewer pores and cracks), and enhanced mechanical integrity (increased tensile strength and ductility).
generation.baseline: SLM-fabricated HEA components produced at ambient chamber temperatures with rapid cooling, high thermal gradients, and higher incidences of fabrication-induced defects.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the preheating intervention is expected to be significant for components with moderate sizes typical of current lab-scale SLM systems; however, for extremely large builds or for alloys with very narrow process windows, the optimal preheat range may vary. Additionally, the preheat must be tuned to avoid undesired phase transformations or coarsening that might occur at excessive temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum preheat temperature range and its interaction with specific alloy compositions and geometries are not currently fully quantified. There is also some uncertainty regarding potential trade-offs between reduced defects and possible alterations in phase stability or grain growth.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA samples using SLM under identical laser parameters and powder feedstock: one set under standard (ambient) chamber conditions and the other with a controlled preheated chamber at selected temperature(s) (e.g., 300 °C). Characterize the components by measuring dimensional deviations using high-resolution optical metrology, microstructural examination via SEM, and mechanical testing (tensile and hardness).
measurements: Dimensional accuracy metrics (deviation from design dimensions)
Defect density and type (quantified by micro-CT or microscopy)
Residual stress profiles (using X-ray diffraction or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% reduction in dimensional deviations and defect density, along with improved mechanical properties) compared to the non-preheated baseline, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this context, the laser power P and scan speed v were the variable parameters, systematically varied to evaluate their influence on the microstructure and mechanical properties (including density, hardness, tensile strength, and impact toughness), enabling the assessment of how modifications in process parameters affect these properties. To investigate the processability and hot cracking susceptibility, the study employs a 3D printer equipped with a relatively low laser power (up to 250 W) compared to most of the available studies that use higher laser power (>250 W) for fabrication of the additively manufactured HEA parts [,].

The study was subject to a few limitations, the foremost of which was the absence of pre-alloyed powder of the desired chemical composition. Thus, mechanical alloyed powder was used instead, which had a few drawbacks of its own. Only small powder quantities with comparatively coarse particle sizes could be established. Therefore, a small PBF-LB machinery able to cope with these conditions was employed, but it lacked the ability to preheat the fabrication chamber. Despite these difficulties, however, the CrFeNiTi MPEA was successfully processed by means of PBF-LB, and samples with large defect-free sections were produced. This serves as a good indicator that this type of alloy is suitable for the PBF-LB process, and with better processing circumstances, significantly larger, defect-free samples should be attainable.
